title: The Unplanned Saturday
description: Your plans cancel and the day is blank. Make six quick Saturday choices and order two sets of day blocks to see how you spend open time.

dimensions.description: Whether open time tends to fill with something you invent or with a ready-made plan someone else offers.
Whether you prefer one long activity or several short tastes of different things.

questions.prompt: Your morning plans cancel at the last minute. What is your first move?
questions.explanation: Both moves fill a blank morning well. This choice only shows whether you start from your own idea or from someone else's open offer.

options.label: Invent a small project of my own
Reply to a friend's standing invitation

questions.prompt: You have a free afternoon, at home or out. How do you shape it?
questions.explanation: Neither shape is better. One long stretch suits deep immersion, while several short ones suit variety. This choice tracks which feels more natural.

options.label: Settle into one activity for hours
Try a handful of short activities

questions.prompt: A free hour opens up near your neighborhood. What sounds better?
questions.explanation: A route you design and a posted community event both make a good hour. Your pick hints at where you want the idea to come from.

options.label: Design my own little route to explore
Join an event already posted nearby

questions.prompt: You want something to watch or play this evening. Which approach fits you?
questions.explanation: Both approaches are legitimate ways to spend an evening. The choice shows whether you like depth in one thing or a quick taste of several.

options.label: Pick one long thing and stay with it
Sample a few short pieces back to back

questions.prompt: The blank day is still blank at noon. What do you do next?
questions.explanation: Starting something nobody asked for and saying yes to a ready-made class are equally fine. This item shows which comes more easily when the day is open.

options.label: Start something nobody asked me to do
Say yes to a class or drop-in session

questions.prompt: Rainy Saturday with a game shelf in reach. Which plan sounds better?
questions.explanation: A single big puzzle rewards sustained focus, while many quick games reward variety. Your pick reflects the rhythm you reach for on an open day.

options.label: One big puzzle, worked on all day
Several quick games, one after another

questions.prompt: Order these Saturday blocks from most to least appealing for your ideal day.
questions.explanation: Each block is a pleasant way to spend time. Where you place them shows the balance of self-started versus invited, and long versus short.

items.label: Build something of my own design
Go along with a friend's plan
Settle into one long, absorbing stretch
Hop between several short things

questions.prompt: Order these full-day formats from the one you would pick first to the one you would pick last.
questions.explanation: Every format here mixes who starts the plan with how long it runs. Your ordering shows which combination you lean toward on an open day.

items.label: Start my own long project
Join a group that rotates through mini sessions
Invent a bunch of small experiments
Follow a host's all-day workshop

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: A playful reflection based only on your choices here. The scenarios are invented, and there are no right or wrong answers or diagnoses.

title: Your Tiny Decision Constitution
description: Draft small decision rules as constitution articles, rank the ones you would defend, and apply them to low-stakes dilemmas like bakeries and notebooks. Your preference scales run from Keep Options Open to Commit Early and from Gut to Evidence.

dimensions.description: Whether your rules favor staying flexible and reversible or settling a choice and moving on.
Whether your rules lean on instinct and feel or on checking facts and comparing reasons first.

questions.prompt: Draft article one. When two options feel equal, which rule would you adopt?
questions.explanation: Choosing the reversible option keeps doors open, while choosing and stopping to reconsider saves mental energy. Both are reasonable rules.

options.label: Pick the one I can undo later
Pick one and stop reconsidering

questions.prompt: Draft article two. How should a small decision begin?
questions.explanation: Trusting a first feeling is fast and personal. Checking one reliable fact adds grounding. This article shows which starting point you would write into law.

options.label: Trust the first feeling that arrives
Check one reliable fact first

questions.prompt: Draft article three. Two friends give opposite tips about where to eat tonight. What is your rule?
questions.explanation: Going with what sits right and tallying reasons both settle the tie. Your choice shows how much structure you want in everyday decisions.

options.label: Go with whichever tip sits right with me
List the reasons for each and compare

questions.prompt: Order these draft articles from the one you would defend most to the one you would defend least.
questions.explanation: All four are workable rules. Your order shows which principles you would protect first when drafting your personal constitution.

items.label: Keep a way back from every choice
Decide once and move on
Listen to my gut
Show the evidence before deciding

questions.prompt: Order these combined articles from your strongest endorsement to your weakest.
questions.explanation: Each article pairs a way of committing with a way of knowing. The ranking shows which pairing feels most like your own rulebook.

items.label: Wait for a hunch before setting any plan
Choose by checklist, then commit
Leave room to change course after testing
Make a gut call and stand by it

questions.prompt: You start a new notebook for lists. Which writing tool does your constitution recommend?
questions.explanation: Pencil keeps entries editable and pen makes them permanent. Neither is better; your pick shows how you apply flexibility to tiny habits.

options.label: Pencil, so I can change any entry
Pen, so I stick with what I wrote

questions.prompt: Two bakeries are near your route and you can only visit one today. How do you decide?
questions.explanation: Heading for the one that feels right and comparing menus and hours are both sensible. Your choice shows whether the rule is instinct or evidence.

options.label: Go to the one that feels right
Compare their menus and hours first

questions.prompt: A hobby club asks you to set a meeting day for the whole season. Which do you propose?
questions.explanation: A rotating schedule keeps flexibility, while a fixed day builds routine. Your proposal shows how your rules treat future plans.

options.label: A flexible rotating schedule
The same day every week

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: A playful self-reflection game using invented low-stakes scenarios. It gives no verdicts about money, health, career or relationships, and its results come only from your choices.

title: Lost in a Cozy Bookshop
description: Wander an invented bookshop with creaky stairs and odd shelves, then decide which details you would keep to reveal how you browse.

dimensions.description: Whether you drift slowly through a shop letting shelves pull you or head quickly toward a target.
Whether your browsing appetite favors the known and comfortable or the unlabeled and unexpected.

questions.prompt: You step into the invented shop, where a staff-pick table glows near the door. What do you do?
questions.explanation: Drifting and heading to a target are both good ways to browse. This choice shows how you set your pace as soon as you enter.

options.label: Stroll without a route and let the shelves pull me
Go straight to the staff-pick table

questions.prompt: A staircase creaks upward to two nooks. Which one do you climb toward?
questions.explanation: A nook of worn favorites offers comfort, while an odd corner promises surprise. Your pick reflects your appetite for the known versus the new.

options.label: The nook of worn familiar favorites
The odd corner of unlabeled shelves

questions.prompt: Two aisles lead onward: one long and winding, one short and straight to the counter. Which do you take?
questions.explanation: The winding aisle suits a slow browse and the straight one suits a quick visit. Both are cozy options, and the choice shows your pace.

options.label: The long winding aisle
The short straight aisle

questions.prompt: Near the window, one shelf holds familiar series and a basket holds mystery parcels wrapped by mood. Which first?
questions.explanation: A familiar series is a comfortable return, and a wrapped mystery is a leap. Your choice shows the taste appetite you bring to browsing.

options.label: The shelf of familiar series
A mystery parcel from the basket

questions.prompt: How long do you usually linger in a shop like this before choosing something?
questions.explanation: There is no ideal length. A long linger and a quick pick are both pleasant ways to browse, and the slider records your usual pace.
questions.highLabel: In and out with a pick

questions.prompt: Order these shop corners from the one you would visit first to the one you would visit last.
questions.explanation: Each corner is part of the shop's charm. Your order combines how slowly you roam with how adventurous your taste is.

items.label: The winding back stairs
The front display table
A shelf of familiar covers
A shelf of puzzling unlabeled spines

questions.prompt: You may keep one feature of the shop in your imagination. Which would you choose?
questions.explanation: A slow creaky staircase and a clear map by the door suit different browsing styles. Your pick shows which pace you cherish.

options.label: The creaking staircase that slows every visit
A clear map by the door showing every section

questions.prompt: Which small shop tradition would you keep for your own visits?
questions.explanation: A shelf for returning to favorites and a jar of random picks both enrich a shop. Your choice shows whether you crave comfort or surprise.

options.label: A shelf for things I want to read again
A jar of random picks I have never heard of

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: The bookshop is invented and names no real books or authors. Results reflect browsing style only and make no judgment about reading habits.

title: The Curiosity Detour
description: Everyday errands keep offering side paths. Choose how deeply you follow leads and whether you explore yourself or ask others, then order your methods.

dimensions.description: Whether you follow one lead all the way or sample several leads briefly.
Whether you prefer to find things out by looking and exploring yourself or by asking people who know.

questions.prompt: Walking to a quick errand, you notice a community hall with a sign saying all welcome and music inside. What next?
questions.explanation: Listening for a long while and taking a short peek are both natural curiosity. Your choice shows how far you follow a single lead.

options.label: Step in and hear the whole piece
Take a brief peek and note other things to try

questions.prompt: A public notice board shows three different flyers. How do you read them?
questions.explanation: Reading one closely or skimming all three are both useful. This item tracks whether your curiosity digs deep or spreads wide.

options.label: Read one flyer thoroughly
Skim all three quickly

questions.prompt: Chalk arrows on a public path branch in several directions. What is your approach?
questions.explanation: Following one arrow to its end or glancing down each branch are equally playful. Your pick reflects depth versus breadth.

options.label: Follow one arrow all the way to its end
Look at the start of each branch

questions.prompt: At a market stall you spot an unfamiliar tool. How do you learn what it is?
questions.explanation: Examining something by hand and asking the seller are both good ways to learn. This choice shows your preferred source of answers.

options.label: Look it over and try it by hand
Ask the seller what it is for

questions.prompt: You hear an unusual sound near a plaza fountain. How do you find out what it is?
questions.explanation: Walking toward a sound and asking a passerby both resolve the mystery. Your choice shows whether you want to discover or consult.

options.label: Walk toward it and work it out myself
Ask someone nearby if they know

questions.prompt: Order these ways of learning about a new neighborhood from most to least like you.
questions.explanation: Observing and exploring are firsthand methods, while asking others is a shared one. Your order shows how you balance them.

items.label: Look closely at what is around me
Ask someone who lives nearby
Walk down a new street to see it
Message a friend who knows the area

questions.prompt: Order these curiosity styles from the one you would try first to the one you would try last.
questions.explanation: These styles mix depth with where answers come from. Your ranking shows which combination fits your sense of curiosity.

items.label: Follow one lead until I understand it
Peek at five leads for a minute each
Trace one mystery on my own
Collect hints from several neighbors

questions.prompt: On a free walk with several interesting leads, how do you spend your attention?
questions.explanation: Staying with one thread and sampling many are both curious. The slider records where you land between depth and breadth.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: These everyday scenarios are invented and kept safe and public. The result describes playful curiosity styles from your choices, not risk-taking or safety judgments.

title: Deadline Triage: Village Festival Edition
description: An invented village festival opens at dusk and not everything will be ready. Order task boards and choose what to protect, drop or hand off.

dimensions.description: Whether you tackle the closest deadline first or the task that benefits the most people.
Whether you tend to power through tasks yourself or spread them among helpers.

questions.prompt: With one hour left, order these festival tasks from what you would tackle first to last.
questions.explanation: Every task matters to the festival. Your order shows whether you start with the nearest deadline or the broadest benefit, and whether you work alone.

items.label: Fix the lantern that must be lit before dusk
Finish the soup most guests will eat
Run the stage test myself
Recruit volunteers to run the stage test

questions.prompt: Order these opening preparations from the one you would start first to the one you would start last.
questions.explanation: These preparations all help the festival. Your order mixes timing, reach, and how much help you would gather.

items.label: Hang the gate sign needed at opening
Set up the welcome table that shapes everyone's first impression
Paint signs alone in a quiet corner
Gather a sign-painting crew

questions.prompt: Order these working styles from the one you would choose first to the one you would choose last.

items.label: Closest deadline first, working alone
Biggest benefit first, working with a team
Closest deadline first, with helpers
Biggest benefit first, working alone

options.label: The job whose deadline is in twenty minutes
The job that matters most to the most guests, due in seventy minutes

questions.prompt: Two things are unfinished. Which one gets your next ten minutes?
questions.explanation: A stair step needed within ten minutes and seating that serves many guests are both worthwhile. Your choice shows urgency versus reach.

Arrange seating that many guests will use later

questions.prompt: The soup needs stirring and the signs need painting. How do you handle both?
questions.explanation: Doing both yourself keeps control, while handing one off frees time. Your choice shows how you tend to carry a load.

options.label: Stir and paint both myself
Hand the signs to a volunteer

questions.prompt: You know the stage test well and a sound volunteer is free. What do you do?
questions.explanation: Keeping a task you know and handing it over with a note are both sensible. This shows how readily you share a load.

options.label: Keep the stage test since I know it
Hand it to the volunteer with a note

questions.prompt: The festival crew offers to help with everything left. How do you respond?
questions.explanation: Finishing alone and splitting the list are both valid responses. Your answer shows your default between pushing solo and sharing the load.

Split my list into thirds and share it

title: Values Auction

dimensions.description: Whether you split tokens across many lots or commit heavily to one.
Whether your tokens go to reliable routines or to new experiences.

A monthly surprise outing

A new-skill class

questions.prompt: Rank these lots by which you would outbid others for, first to last.

Monthly day trip

questions.explanation: Where leftover tokens land shows your tie-breaking instinct between dependable comforts and something new.

Whether a place feels yours through private space or through the people who share it.

title: Name That Decision Trap
description: Match everyday stories to the names of common decision traps using short definitions, then choose how you would act in four scenarios. Your matching accuracy is scored separately from your preference scales, which run from Cautious to Trusting and from Past-Pull to Future-Pull.

sections.title: Your own picks
sections.description: Preference scenarios with no right answers.

dimensions.description: Whether you tend to verify and hedge before committing, or go with what is offered and commit quickly.
Whether earlier effort, habit and track record weigh more in your choice, or what might happen next.

questions.prompt: Match each story to the decision trap it shows.
questions.context: Sunk cost: continuing because of effort or money already spent and unrecoverable. Anchoring: a first number pulls later estimates toward it. Status quo bias: favoring the current option just because it is current. Confirmation bias: favoring evidence that supports what you already believe.

left.label: Ravi pays for a full year of gym classes, hates them, and keeps going so the fee is not wasted.
Mei sees a jacket marked down from 300 to 180 and calls it a bargain without checking other shops.
Tomás keeps his old phone plan, though an equal cheaper one exists, because it is what he has always had.

questions.explanation: Ravi is driven by money already gone, Mei by the first price she saw, and Tomás by familiarity alone. No story shows someone filtering evidence to fit a belief.

questions.prompt: Match each story to the trap it illustrates.
questions.context: Availability bias: judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. Confirmation bias: seeking only evidence that supports a belief you hold. Framing effect: reacting differently to identical facts depending on wording. Bandwagon effect: choosing something because many others do.

left.label: After seeing news about one delayed flight, Lena decides flights are almost always late this month.
Kofi reads only the glowing reviews of the laptop he already wants and skips the critical ones.
Aiko likes a course advertised as '80% of students pass' but would avoid it if it said '20% of students fail'.

questions.explanation: Lena's vivid news memory inflates her estimate, Kofi filters for agreement, and Aiko reacts to wording even though 80% pass and 20% fail are the same fact.

questions.prompt: Which trap does each story show?
questions.context: Planning fallacy: underestimating your own time or cost despite past overruns. Loss aversion: a loss weighs more than an equal gain. Hindsight bias: feeling an outcome was obvious after learning it. Gambler's fallacy: expecting a streak in independent chance events to reverse.

left.label: Nia expects to finish a report in two hours, though her last three took about six each.
Dev refuses a bet to win 120 or lose 100 because the possible loss bothers him more than the gain attracts him.
After the match, Sam insists he knew the underdog would win, though he was unsure beforehand.

questions.explanation: Nia ignores her own track record, Dev weighs losses heavily, and Sam rewrites his earlier uncertainty. Nobody here expects a chance streak to reverse.

questions.prompt: Match each story to a trap. Some traps appear more than once.
questions.context: Bandwagon effect: choosing something because many others do. Halo effect: one impressive trait colors judgment of unrelated traits. Survivorship bias: studying only visible successes and ignoring those that dropped out of view.

left.label: Parisa joins a long restaurant queue only because she assumes a long line means great food.
Hana buys a hoodie because suddenly everyone in her class is wearing one.
Kwame trusts a startup tactic after reading only about famous founders who used it, ignoring the many who tried it and quit.
Elena trusts a coworker's spreadsheet figures mainly because his presentation was polished.

questions.explanation: Parisa and Hana follow the crowd. Kwame only sees survivors. Elena lets presentation polish vouch for unrelated accuracy, which is the halo effect.

questions.prompt: You have spent three months on a tedious language course, and a promising new one appears. What do you do?
questions.context: This scenario is invented. There is no right answer; your pick only moves your two preference scales.

options.label: Finish the old course first, then try the new one.

Try a free sample lesson of the new course before deciding.

questions.explanation: This scenario resembles sunk cost. Your choice is a style preference showing how much weight you give to past effort versus verification.

questions.prompt: A used bike is listed at 400. You have no firm idea of its worth. What is your move?
questions.context: This scenario is invented. Every option is a reasonable style; none is scored.

options.label: Compare three similar listings before offering anything.

Ask the seller about its history and take their word.
Wait a week to see if the price drops or better ones appear.

questions.explanation: A listed price can act as an anchor. Your answer shows whether you check existing information, trust the seller, or lean on what might come next.

questions.prompt: An unfamiliar company offers a cheaper plan than your current one. How do you respond?
questions.context: This scenario is invented. Cheaper is the only fact you know about the new plan.

options.label: Stay put; the current plan has served me well.
Sign up now; the offer sounds good.
Read independent write-ups and trial it for a month first.
Stay, because people I know recommend the current one.

questions.explanation: This echoes status quo bias. Your pick is a preference about how you weigh familiarity, other people's views and future gains, not a skill result.

questions.prompt: Your team is moving to a new project tool because everyone else seems to like it. Rank these responses from most to least appealing to you.
questions.context: This scenario is invented. Assume no one has given hard evidence either way. There is no right order; your ranking only moves your two preference scales.

items.label: Join in, since the team consensus points that way.
Request a demo and pilot it on one small task first.
Keep the proven tool until someone shows a clear reason.
Join; our past team choices have mostly worked out.

questions.explanation: This scenario touches the bandwagon effect. Your ranking maps your preferences: responses you place higher count more toward their style, whether that is going with the group or trusting track record (Trusting), piloting first or keeping the proven tool (Cautious), and leaning on past results (Past-Pull) or on what the new tool might bring (Future-Pull).

note: All stories and scenarios are invented. Definitions are short game summaries, not formal research claims. The knowledge score counts only matching accuracy; the preference scales reflect your choices, are not scored, and are not a diagnosis.

title: The Repair Café Dilemmas

dimensions.description: Whether you lean toward bringing a broken thing back to how it was made or toward changing its look or giving it a new use.

questions.prompt: A visitor brings a wooden stool with one cracked leg. Which plan appeals to you most?

Work out with the table how best to mend the original leg, matching its shape together
Lay out the broken leg and the offcuts and let the table brainstorm what the stool could become

title: Your Kind of Haunted House
description: Build a fictional haunted-house evening through atmosphere choices, rankings and tradeoffs. See where your choices fall between welcoming and uncanny, and watching and participating.

questions.prompt: You can set the mood of the first room. Which invitation would you rather walk into?
questions.explanation: These choices describe the atmosphere you prefer here, not how brave or anxious you are.

options.label: A warm lamp, an old armchair and a ghost who seems pleased to see you
A familiar hallway with one impossible detail: every reflection arrives a moment late

questions.prompt: Rank these ways to spend the first ten minutes, most appealing first.
questions.explanation: The order combines your taste for gentle or uncanny scenes with whether you watch or participate.

items.label: Listen beside the fire while a host tells a gentle ghost story
Help a friendly ghost choose a final line for its story
Watch an unsettling scene unfold through a one-way stage window
Enter an uncanny scene and answer when the unseen host calls your name

questions.prompt: A performer offers you a part in the next scene. Both versions tell the same story. Which do you choose?
questions.explanation: Watching a performance and taking a role are equally valid ways to enjoy it.

options.label: A seat with a clear view; let the performers carry the scene
A small speaking role; let me help the scene happen

questions.prompt: Where would you set the atmosphere for the next room?
questions.explanation: This is your chosen setting for this fictional visit, not a measure of fear tolerance.

questions.prompt: For each moment, choose whether you would rather watch it or take part.
questions.explanation: You can reuse either approach. The choices contribute only to the participation scale.
questions.context: All scenes are fictional, staged and optional. Each has both a seated spectator version and a willing-participant version.

left.label: A ghost reads an unfinished letter
A portrait asks a visitor a question
The cast invites someone to deliver the closing line

questions.prompt: You can keep only one of these two rooms in your evening. Which tradeoff would you take?
questions.explanation: This deliberately trades atmosphere against participation; it does not label one option more adventurous.

options.label: A welcoming room where you help a ghost finish a ritual of farewell
An uncanny room where you quietly watch a story you cannot quite explain

questions.prompt: Rank these final scenes from the ending you would choose first to the one you would choose last.
questions.explanation: The ending preferences add another view of atmosphere and participation, without assigning a personality type.

items.label: Watch a ghost reunite with an old friend beside a bright window
Join the farewell and help read the friend's name aloud
Watch a darkened stage empty itself while one shadow remains
Step into the last scene and answer the remaining shadow

questions.prompt: For a future visit like this, how much would you want to participate?
questions.explanation: Your two scales summarize choices made here. They are original entertainment descriptions, not a validated assessment.

title: The Role Behind Your Mask
description: At a fictional Halloween masquerade, choose what to reveal, what to prepare and what to invent in the moment. Discover the kind of role you would actually want to play.

questions.prompt: You are entrusted with the missing heir’s invitation. How would you most enjoy putting it into the story?
questions.explanation: This choice places your preferred version of this scene along Private Thread–Shared Spotlight. Intimate exchanges and a room-wide moment offer different kinds of involvement.
questions.context: Original fictional masquerade: you play a courier at a house whose absent heir may return tonight. Each version moves the story forward; the tradeoff is who shares the discovery.

options.label: Arrange a charged meeting with one guest; the rest of the room may never know
Let a small circle uncover it, then decide together whether to announce it
Interrupt the masked reception with a reveal everyone can react to

questions.prompt: You can shape your courier’s entrance. Which freedom would you choose?
questions.explanation: This choice places your preferred version of this scene along Prepared Scene–Live Improvisation. Preparation offers a crafted shape; improvisation offers room to respond.
questions.context: Original scene: all three versions give you the same important role and the same speaking time. You decide how much of it exists before the doors open.

options.label: Write a precise entrance and practise it; keep the wording when the room gets noisy
Prepare an opening line and a few facts, leaving the exchange open
Know only what the courier wants and invent the entrance from what guests do

questions.prompt: Rank the roles you would most want for the next scene, most appealing first.
questions.explanation: This ranking contributes only to Private Thread–Shared Spotlight. Every role has agency; the difference is the size of the moment you share.
questions.context: Original scene: a borrowed family name has opened the wrong door. All three roles can uncover what happened, but you can take only one.

items.label: The confidant who pursues one guest’s hidden reason for borrowing the name
The table host who draws three guests’ conflicting accounts into one conversation
The herald who brings the disputed identity before the whole gathering

questions.prompt: Only one version of your discovery can be staged. Which would feel most rewarding?
questions.explanation: This choice places your preferred version of this scene along Private Thread–Shared Spotlight. Intimate exchanges and a room-wide moment offer different kinds of involvement.
questions.context: Original scene: you have found an old invitation that changes why the heir stayed away. All versions disclose the same fictional information; none exposes a real person’s secret. A wider audience costs you the intimate exchange.

options.label: Give the heir a private chance to respond, keeping that conversation between you
Let your table hear the response, then carry a short account to the room
Ask the heir in front of everyone, letting the whole gathering witness the response

questions.prompt: Your scene partner offers a surprising explanation for the old invitation. What working arrangement would you prefer?
questions.explanation: This choice places your preferred version of this scene along Prepared Scene–Live Improvisation. Preparation offers a crafted shape; improvisation offers room to respond.
questions.context: Original scene: you and your partner have equal say. The audience and stakes stay the same; you choose the balance between a shaped payoff and discovery while performing.

options.label: Agree on the explanation before performing, so the clues lead to a deliberate ending
Keep an agreed ending but invent how your characters reach it
Let the explanation arrive during the scene and build the ending together

questions.prompt: Rank these ways of creating a final exchange, most appealing first.
questions.explanation: This ranking contributes only to Prepared Scene–Live Improvisation. It compares different ways of making the same small scene, with no skill judgment.
questions.context: Original scene: you will perform a two-person farewell. Each option has the same audience and importance.

items.label: Rehearse the exchange until a small repeated gesture carries the ending
Agree on the final gesture, but leave the words open
Discover both words and gesture by responding to your partner in the moment

questions.prompt: How would you divide your final scene between a private thread and a shared spotlight?
questions.explanation: The slider describes where you would place the evening’s final attention. A middle position can preserve both kinds of connection.
questions.context: Original scene: your courier must return the invitation. Imagine a continuum from an exchange noticed by one other character to a farewell witnessed by the room.

questions.prompt: How much of your next masquerade role would you want to discover while playing it?
questions.explanation: This final choice contributes to Prepared Scene–Live Improvisation. Your result combines four contributions per scale; it describes your choices tonight, not a fixed identity.
questions.context: Original reflection: keep the role and audience you want. Only change how much you settle beforehand.

sources.label: Original masquerade scenes and descriptive preference mappings, authored for TypologyQuiz

note: Original fiction. All roles involve active participation; these choices concern how you shape a scene, not bravery or sociability. Results describe this attempt only: no diagnosis, validated personality type or better pole. Each dimension receives four equally weighted task contributions.

dimensions.description: Private Thread favours discoveries exchanged with a few people; Shared Spotlight favours moments the room can experience together. Either can involve leadership, invention and connection.
Prepared Scene favours shaping details in advance; Live Improvisation favours shaping them in response to others. Neither indicates greater creativity or competence.

title: Costume Tradeoff Workshop
description: Make eight concrete costume decisions from supplied fictional character sketches. Compare a reusable foundation with a one-night transformation, and a faithful cue with a personal reading; neither approach earns a better result.

dimensions.description: How much of a costume plan you would build around using its base again versus changing it substantially for one role.
Whether you would keep a recognizable cue from a character or reshape what that cue means.

sections.title: Start with what is on the rack
sections.description: Choose a base and a character cue without altering anyone else’s property.

sections.title: Make it work in the room

sources.label: Original fictional costume workshop scenarios

note: Fictional sketches are described in text. All costume bases and props are owned or used with stated permission. Results describe these decisions only; they do not measure creativity, skill, or personality.

questions.prompt: The sketch of a fictional night watch shows a charcoal coat and tall silver collar. Which coat plan would you pick?
questions.context: A friend offers a plain coat on the condition that it stays unchanged. You also own an older charcoal coat and may alter it. Either plan can carry the same removable silver collar from the sketch.
questions.explanation: Both builds honor ownership and keep the character cue. The first preserves a wearable borrowed base; the second changes a coat you own for one night.

options.label: Borrow the friend’s coat unchanged and add the removable collar
Tailor your own older coat for this one role and add the same collar

questions.prompt: The storm cartographer sketch has a compass rose on the shoulder. What should your removable travel panel say about the character?
questions.context: Your own plain jacket stays intact and the panel comes off before a crowded bus ride. Both designs stay flat and removable.
questions.explanation: The same practical panel solves the bus constraint. The choice changes the story of its symbol, from the supplied compass to your weather-map reading.

options.label: Keep the sketch’s compass rose as the clear character cue
Draw cloud paths across the panel to recast the cartographer as someone who maps weather

questions.prompt: Rank three ways to build the fictional bell keeper’s costume from the one you would most enjoy to the one you would least enjoy.
questions.context: The sketch shows a dark jacket and a small bell emblem. The jacket is yours. Every plan keeps that emblem visible, and each gives a complete costume for the evening.
questions.explanation: This ranking records how much change you want to make to a garment you own. The familiar bell remains in every plan; it is not a creativity contest.

items.label: Wear your jacket unchanged with a removable bell emblem
Add a removable shaped outer layer over your jacket and the bell emblem
Reshape your own jacket for this role and keep the bell emblem

questions.prompt: A long cape in the moth librarian sketch catches on dinner chairs. You remove the cape. Which shorter replacement would you choose?
questions.context: Both options use a short, detachable shoulder piece that clears the chair backs. The remaining sketch shows moth antennae; page-like seams would be your own reading of the librarian.
questions.explanation: The cape is gone in both complete fixes. One keeps the sketch’s moth cue; the other lets the librarian’s books carry the cue.

options.label: Keep the antennae as the shoulder piece’s visible character cue
Use page-like seams on the shoulder piece to read the character through books

questions.prompt: The keeper of lost keys sketch includes a lantern, but a borrowed prop is too glaring for this room. Which complete prop plan appeals?
questions.context: The owner permits a removable glare-reducing cover but no changes to the borrowed prop. Your own already-dim prop can be changed for this event. Both versions display the same brass-key cue from the sketch.
questions.explanation: Both choices solve the glare as stated and respect the borrowed prop. The distinction is whether the base remains reusable or an owned prop becomes a one-night build.

options.label: Keep the borrowed prop unchanged under its permitted removable cover, with a key emblem
Use your own already-dim prop, reshaped for this role with the same key emblem

questions.prompt: Rank the details you would most want on a detachable badge for the fictional lighthouse keeper.
questions.context: The supplied sketch has a small reflective lighthouse badge. Your version may explain the keeper through a boat route or a rescue note instead. The same owned coat and detachable badge work with all three details.
questions.explanation: This ranking compares a supplied visual cue with two readings of what the keeper does. The shared coat and badge leave the garment decision out of this task.

items.label: The lighthouse silhouette from the sketch
A line of boats approaching the light
A tiny “come home” note in place of the tower image

questions.lowLabel: Build around a base I can wear again
questions.highLabel: Build a substantially changed look for this role
questions.prompt: For a future costume, where would you place the balance between a reusable base and a one-night transformation?
questions.explanation: The endpoints name two reasonable approaches. The position is descriptive and does not imply a better costume or a more capable maker.

questions.prompt: When a costume refers to a character or familiar idea, how much would you want to reshape that reference?
questions.explanation: This records a preference for this scenario only; it does not measure creativity or character knowledge.

title: The Last Porch Walk
description: Take a fictional Halloween trick-or-treat circuit from first sweet to final porch. Your choices describe how you spend time on the route and whether moments stay with one person or become group memories.

dimensions.description: How these picks balance spending time at a chosen stop with seeing more of the available circuit.
How these picks balance a moment centered on one person’s experience with an experience composed by the walking group.

sources.label: Original fictional neighborhood walk and descriptive choice scales, written for this quiz.

note: An original fictional walk. Both axes describe choices made here; they do not measure personality, generosity, or social skill.

questions.prompt: The first porch offers wrapped sweets and a tiny hand-drawn maze on each wrapper. Your group can visit either street before curfew. Where do you start?
questions.context: Both streets have welcoming porches and the same walking distance.

options.label: Choose this porch and solve a wrapper maze together before the next stop
Take a sweet and begin the full loop while the other porches are lit

questions.explanation: One choice gives the first treat its own scene; the other begins the larger circuit. Neither changes the number of sweets anyone may take.

questions.prompt: The person handing out sweets admires your friend’s hand-painted paper crown. Who would you draw into this one encounter?
questions.context: Your friend is happy either to speak for themselves or to let the group join in.

options.label: Make room for your friend to tell the crown’s short origin to the host
Invite the walkers to name the costume details they each contributed

questions.explanation: This choice records whether the encounter centers one person’s story or becomes a group account.

questions.prompt: Rank which extra you would reach for first—and let it shape the rest of your walk.
questions.context: One porch offers three free paper extras beside the sweets. There is room in your bag for any of them.

items.label: A foldout of this porch’s shadow scene, with a space to invent its last panel
A blank paper flag to add to your costume
A route card that gathers a different small stamp at several porches

questions.explanation: The foldout invites a small project centered on one place; the stamp card gives a reason to visit several places. The flag leaves the route open.

questions.prompt: Two walkers planned a group costume photo, but one now wants to reach a porch where their cousin is handing out treats. How would you change the invitation?
questions.context: Everyone can still meet at the corner afterward; no one is being left behind.

options.label: Offer to accompany that walker to the cousin’s porch, then rejoin the photo
Ask the whole group whether to move the photo to that porch

questions.explanation: Both make space for the changed wish. One starts with a companion; the other remakes a group plan.

questions.prompt: A neighbour gives you a tip: a block ahead has handmade paper treat bags, while the current porch has a story behind its carved sign. How would you spend the next ten minutes?
questions.context: The tip is reliable and both stops remain open. This describes your route, not a better strategy.
questions.lowLabel: Hear the sign’s story before leaving
questions.highLabel: Use the tip to visit the extra block
questions.explanation: A single span of time can be given to the present porch or to another part of the circuit.

questions.prompt: At the paper-bag porch, a friend finds a folded thank-you note slipped in with their sweet. The host asks if you would add a line to the porch memory book. What do you write?
questions.context: The host welcomes either kind of note; this is not a test of gratitude.

options.label: Recall the small joke you shared with the host as the bag was handed over
Record the group’s favourite moment from this block in one joint line

questions.explanation: The same porch can be remembered through a single exchange or a shared account.

questions.prompt: The final ten minutes leave time for one last choice. Which ending would you take?
questions.context: You already have treats; neither route promises more or better ones.

options.label: Return to the wrapper-maze porch and ask how the host designed it
Circle the still-lit side street and see one new doorway before heading home

questions.explanation: The last stop can turn a sweet into a maker’s story, or add one more doorway to the circuit. Either ending is available whichever route you began with.

questions.prompt: Back at the corner, you can keep one trace of tonight. What would make the best ending?
questions.context: Imagine a simple paper keepsake; the quiz records only your selection, not a photo or saved story.
questions.lowLabel: Keep the maze wrapper as your own reminder
questions.highLabel: Write a group caption on the back of the route card
questions.explanation: The close moves from a personal memento to a memory the walking group composes together.
